content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposed weighted optimization trajectories (WOT) that refines the optimization trajectories of adversarial training in time to improve robust generalization. Similar to SWA, it used the weighted average of the trajectories other than a particular checkpoint for inference. The main idea of the proposed algorithm is to use a small validation set to optimize the weight of the training trajectories.

This paper considered two variants of WOT:

WOT-W: Consider the whole trajectories.

WOT-B: Split the trajectories into several blocks.

The authors provided comprehensive experiments to study the performance of WOT.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

Overall, the paper is well-written and easy to follow. The proposed algorithm looks reasonable. It is shown that SWA can find flat minima to improve robust generalization. Intuitively, WOT may find flatter minima to improve robust generalization since the weight is carefully chosen, as it is discussed in Sec. 3.

Weakness:

I mainly have three concerns about the proposed algorithms.

1, I think the proposed method is a little bit lack of novelty. $\alpha_i$ is essentially equivalent to the SWA learning rate, which is a hyperparameter when using SWA. The proposed method uses a small unseen dataset to optimize the hyperparameters. This is a common idea in machine learning community.

2, In Table 2, in the experiments on WRN-34-10, Trades+SWA is much worse than Trades. It is a little counterintuitive. To my knowledge, some of the models ranking at the top of Robustbench are implemented using trades+swa. In my own experiments, I have tried both torch.optim.swa_utils and the class WATrainer (implementation of the [1,2]). Using both packages, Trades + SWA is better than Trades. It seems that the code is adopted from the experiments of Rice et al., 2020, and I find no bugs in the implementation. I wonder whether it is due to the training settings or the implementation of SWA. Since the proposed algorithm is related to SWA, this is an important issue.

3, Memory cost and performance trade-off. The main issue of the algorithm is that it requires storing k=n/m models. SWA only requires storing two models. This issue limits the further implementation of the large-scale model in practice. The current improved performance is not strong enough to cover the huge memorization cost.

[1] Gowal, Sven and Qin, Chongli and Uesato, Jonathan and Mann, Timothy and Kohli, Pushmeet, Uncovering the Limits of Adversarial Training against Norm-Bounded Adversarial Examples.

[2] Rebuffi, Sylvestre-Alvise and Gowal, Sven and Calian, Dan A. and Stimberg, Florian and Wiles, Olivia and Mann, Timothy, Fixing Data Augmentation to Improve Adversarial Robustness.


Minor: 

Even though the paper is well-written. It still contains few typos. For example,

Sec. 2,$ \sum_i$ (AT, Trades, and MART) and $\sum_1$ (AWP) are inconsistent.
Sec. 3.1, 
after the i-th optimization step.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes an optimization strategy to improve the robustness of adversarial training (AD). AD algorithms are known to overfit to the training set and do not perform well on unseen data. This work proposes to create a new model at the end of training where weights are set to a weighted average of their values along training. The coefficients for the average are learnt by optimizing them on a held-out validation set. The algorithms is called weighted optimization trajectories (WOT) and is proposed in two variations. WOT-W uses the same coefficients for all weights at a given timestamp. WOT-B uses different coefficients for different blocks of the model even at the same time stamp.

Results are shown on different datasets (SVHN, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet), different architectures VGG16, Wide Resnet-34-10, and PreAct Resnet-18), different attacks (L-inf, L_2, PDG-20, PDG-100, CW_inf) and different baseline algorithms (AT, Trades, AWP+AT, MART, SWA). Results show consistent improvements over state of the art algorithms in all settings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
- The proposed algorithm show consistent improvements in a wide variety of settings (different architectures and attacks and algorithms).
- The paper is clear and details for reproducibility are shared (including code)

Weaknesses
The main weakness of this work are the limited novelty, marginal improvements, and potentially some unfair comparisons.

- Limited novelty: Novelty is limited to the use of learnt coefficients for performing the averaging of the weight trajectories. Averaging trajectory in order to obtain a smoother optimization landscape and wider minima has already been proposed a few times, e.g., “Averaging Weights Leads to Wider Optima and Better Generalization” [Izmailov 2018] (SWA) and its application to adversarial attack too , e.g., “Boosting Certified l_inf Robustness with EMA Method and Ensemble Model” [Li et al. 2021]. Averaging trained models as a form of ensemble continues to be a popular choice, e.g., “Model soups: averaging weights of multiple fine-tuned models improves accuracy without increasing inference time” Wortsman et all ICML2022.
- Improvements are consistent across attacks and architectures but marginal (on average around 1%? I did not compute it exactly but it seems on that order) at the added complexity of setting up an extra optimization procedure, and additional memory needed to store all weights across time, and compute cost (albeit limited according to the information in the appendix).
- Finally the some comparison might be unfair. If I understand correctly, the models for the proposed technique were exposed to an additional validation set while the rest of the algorithms were not. For fair comparison all algorithms tested should also benefit from a similar advantage. I’d encourage to provide all the results for the other algorithms similarly to what is done in table 5 for the SWA algorithm where its hyper-parameters were also optimized on the validation set. For algorithms there fine tuning hyper parameters might not be doable I’d consider:
    - Use the validation for fine tuning the weights
    - Use the validation for fine tuning just the batch norm weights (if batch norm is used)
    - Incorporate the validation in the training set
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is overall clear and details seems to be all provided between the paper and the appendix. The authors have also shared their code. The novelty is quite limited.

Some comments to further improve clarity:
- I would encourage the authors to define what robustness means in this setting from the very beginning. There are many form of robustness: to distribution shifts, to spurious correlations, to artificial adversarial data, to natural adversarial data. It is unclear until late in the paper what “ROBUST GENERALIZATION” (and robust overfitting) means unless the reader is familiar with the literature.
- This sounds like a very strong statement: “adversarial training has become the de facto method for improving robustness of deep neural networks” I’d be bit more cautious and tone this statement down a bit. For example see this quote from [Measuring Robustness to Natural Distribution Shifts in Image Classification, Nuerisp2020] “For consistency shifts, adversarially trained models generally have effective robustness, but usually little or no relative robustness. On ImageNet-Vid-Robust, the baseline models without adversarial training still achieve higher accuracy under distribution shift. “. In the body of the paper this sentence has been rephrased more specifically for adversarial robustness which might be more appropriate. I invite the author to adopt the same phrasing for the abstract.
- Information on the extra cost is present in the appendix but I believe is key to convince someone to adopt this strategy. I’d encourage the authors to fit it in the main paper if possible
content.summary_of_the_review: The novelty of the proposed technique is quite limited (learning the coefficient for the averaging). Averaging weights is known to increase robustness [Izmailov 2018], even its application to adversarial attacks [Li et al. 2021]. The results presented show that learning such coefficient does seem to have a consistent advantage over other strategies, however, the gain is marginal and comes at the cost of an additional optimization procedure. I appreciate the clarity and the number of experiments reported, I think the paper could be interesting to reinforce an existing knowledge (the benefit of averaging) but I am not sure the technique is adding new knowledge nor is practical from a cost-benefit perspective.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an approach to learn to weigh the optimization trajectories, as well as each block of the network, and shows superior performance w.r.t. previous work.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+: The block-wise weighting provides incremental improvement in adversarial robustness.

-: The explanation on why this algorithm works might be quite off.

-: Fig. 6 should be compared with SWA instead of the regular baseline.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is written clearly.

The novelty is pretty incremental because the only change is that they tried to learn some weights on the optimization trajectory and each block.

The experiments were well-done with good quality.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I am not very convinced that adding a learnable weight to the SWA trajectory would bring any good over regular adversarial learning, because those knobs were well within the optimization process of a regular adversarial learning procedure. This is kinda proven in the experiments where WOT_W mostly not outperforming regular SWA. WOT-B, instead, which adds a weight per block, might actually be a real useful trick. However, the paper was written in a way to mostly promote WOT itself, which is not very convincing to me. I would e.g. like to see a baseline of:

Not adding any weight to the trajectory (just perform regular SWA) and only add weights to the blocks.

This would really illustrate which part of the algorithm has helped. 

The authors also didn't do much in terms of explaining, either theoretically or empirically, why would their method work. The main explanation comes from Fig. 6, in that they tried to establish that WOT has flatter local minima than the baseline. However, because their method is an extension to SWA, which does the same thing (getting flatter local minima), they should really compare against SWA on this one. In fact, I doubt whether they would outperform SWA by much on this metric, because WOT-W and WOT-B have similar curves but quite different performance.

Overall, my rating would be slightly leaning towards rejection because 1) this is in general a couple of small tweaks to SWA; 2) the writing has been mostly tilted towards promoting WOT-W, but in reality the thing that significantly outperform SWA is WOT-B; 3) it is not clearly explained whether adding alpha to the trajectories is useful or not, or maybe the block-wise weights would be good enough on their own.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
